title: Hatred never ceases by hatred
hook: a comment-section fight where every reply makes it worse, and an old rule
tomorrow: if the whole teaching fit in one verse, what would it say?

segments.voice: Yesterday, the first verse: manopubbangama dhamma, mind goes before, like the wheel behind the ox. And behind it, a week of lines: I undertake the training, five trainings, may all beings be happy, the funeral verse, all formations pass. They come back as a round today, with one more verse to close the week.
screen: `MIND GOES BEFORE.` → `A WEEK OF LINES COMES BACK.`

segments.voice: A comment-section fight. Someone posts something sharp, someone answers sharper, and every reply, however clever, makes the thread longer and hotter. Nobody has ever won one of those by being angrier. So, yesterday's question, can anger be ended by more anger? The Dhammapada answers in its fifth verse, and Pali has a line for it short enough to remember: na hi verena verani.
screen: `EVERY REPLY MAKES IT WORSE.` → `MORE ANGER TO END ANGER?` → `NA HI VERENA VERANI.`

segments.voice: Na hi: not, truly. Verena: by hatred. Verani: hatreds. Not by hatred are hatreds ended. In Max Müller's English the whole verse reads: "For hatred does not cease by hatred at any time: hatred ceases by love—this is an old rule." The verses just before it name the fuel: he insulted me, he hit me, he beat me, he robbed me. Whoever keeps turning those thoughts over, the verses say, keeps the hatred alive. The verse never says who has to stop first. It only says how it stops. And listen for a familiar word at the end. An old rule, in Pali, is dhammo sanantano. Dhamma again, this time meaning a law, the way things work. You've now heard it as the teaching, as things that mind goes before, and as a rule older than any feud. That's the round: one small verse, and a week of lines underneath it.
screen: `NA HI VERENA VERANI.` · `HATRED CEASES BY LOVE.` · `THE FUEL: HE INSULTED ME.` · `DHAMMA AGAIN: AN OLD RULE.` · then, large: `NA HI VERENA VERANI.`

segments.voice: Rest one hand on your chest. Let someone you're at odds with come to mind, or, if that's too much today, just a small grudge. Say the line once, out loud, meaning it as much as you can: na hi verena verani. Then let the hand stay where it is and breathe.
Hatred never ceases by hatred. Na hi verena verani: hatred ends by non-hatred, an old rule. Word sixteen of a little Pali.
screen: `HATRED NEVER CEASES BY HATRED — today's word`.

segments.voice: Keep this one for the week: na hi verena verani, and someone has to stop first. Sixteen days of Pali.

howItsDone: Dhammapada 5 is one of the verses Theravada teachers return to when talking about anger and forgiveness, and some people learn its Pali by heart.

fork.setup: a friend's grandmother has died, and she asks for a Pali line from your week. which one was first spoken at a passing?
fork.reveal: the funeral verse: impermanent, truly, are formations. in the Mahaparinibbana Sutta, Sakka speaks it when the Buddha passes, and its last line turns to ease.

original.note: na hi verena verani in Devanagari letters: not by hatred are hatreds ended (Dhammapada 5).

trapdoor: what you thought: be nice and people will be nice back.
what it means: hatred isn't ended by hatred; it ends by non-hatred, whatever the other side does.
what a scholar hears: avera, non-hatred, which Müller renders 'love', and esa dhammo sanantano, 'this is an old rule': dhamma as a law of how things work.
guess: an old rule: hatred ends only by non-hatred
a rule that hatred ends when both sides win
a curse on those who start the first fight

chat.says: saw the juice kid at class. he wouldn't look at me. do i wait for him to say sorry first?
options: Go first. Na hi verena verani: hatred doesn't end by more of it. Keep it small and kind.
Wait. He spilled first, so by the old rule he's the one who apologizes first.
Ignore him back for a week. That's fair, and after that you're even.
chat.meaning: Dhammapada 5: hatred never ends by hatred, only by non-hatred. It doesn't wait for the other side, so someone has to stop first.
